docs.title: Vergil
docs.text:
Vergil is a fleet-management and repository-governance system: a Python toolchain (vergil-tooling), a Claude Code behavioral plugin, reusable CI/CD actions, and isolated container/VM environments — all coordinated by a two-tier epic / task planning model.

This site is the project's home: what Vergil is, where it's going, and what's shipped recently.

docs.title: Where the project is going
docs.text: The Roadmap is generated from the open epics across every repo in the organization — one view of every cross-cutting initiative, refreshed automatically.

docs.title: What's shipping
docs.text: The Activity log is the by-date record of recently closed work across the whole org.

docs.title: Supported languages
docs.text: Vergil validates repositories across a set of first-class, containerized, multi-version languages — Python, Go, Rust, C++, and now TypeScript (Node.js runtime, single canonical tsc, npm, Vitest + V8 100% coverage, a shareable strict base tsconfig, node-26 / node-24 / node-22 images). See Supported languages for the fleet-level summary.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Every repository in the fleet runs the same CI model, and it is version-agnostic by design: the set of language versions a repo tests against is configuration, not workflow code, and the merge gates never name a version. The versions come from a fleet-wide version window, so a new or dropped language version reaches every repo without an edit; nothing about the workflows or the branch protection has to move with it.

This page is the fleet-level summary. The authoritative mechanics — job names, the reusable-workflow inputs, the evidence bundle format — live in vergil-tooling and are linked below rather than restated here:

  • CI Architecture
  • CI Evidence Convention

docs.title: The version set comes from the version window
docs.text:
A repo's CI version matrix is not embedded in ci.yml and not passed as a workflow input. It comes from the version window, the set of language versions Vergil supports, through one chain:

  1. The manifest. vergil-containers records each language's window in docker/versions/manifest.yml. Every version list in that repo is generated from it.
  2. The published window. The generator also writes docker/versions/window.json, which consumers read at the v2.1 ref.
  3. The resolver. vrg-ci-resolve, in vergil-tooling, reads the window and the repo's vergil.toml and returns the versions to build. Every CI run uses it, through the vergil-actions CI setup, and so does local validation. The matrix fans out over what it returns — a dynamic matrix.

What the resolver returns depends on the repo:

  • No pin. With no [ci].versions, a repo follows the window. A library ([project].repository-type) builds every version in the window. Any other repository type is an app, and builds one version: the newest.
  • [ci].versions is an optional pin. A pinned version that is not in the window is a fatal error, and so is an app pin with more than one version. A pin is visible technical debt, not the normal way to choose versions.

The window moves on its own. A nightly lifecycle job in vergil-containers compares each language's window with its upstream's release and end-of-life data, and opens the add, drop and runtime pull requests that change it (see Nightly governance). A repo that does not pin picks up the change on its next run, with no edit of its own, and no ci.yml is hand-edited, so the matrix cannot drift from the window.

The window, the pin rules and the lifecycle rules are documented once, in vergil-containers' Language version lifecycle page.

docs.title: Thin-caller ci.yml
docs.text:
A consuming repo's ci.yml is a thin caller. Each job simply uses: a vergil-actions reusable workflow at the pinned @v2.1 tag and passes only language: and container-suffix:. It passes no version matrix and no container tag — both resolve dynamically: the matrix from the version window (or from the [ci].versions pin, if one is set), and the single-container jobs' image tag from the primary version (below).

Because the matrix and the container tag are derived rather than written down, the same short workflow serves every repo, and a version change takes effect fleet-wide without touching a single ci.yml.

One exception to "pass only language: and container-suffix:": a repo that publishes packages (see Release packaging) must call the release workflow with secrets: inherit. Its signing secrets are environment secrets, and an explicit secrets: map does not deliver environment secrets to a cross-repo reusable workflow — only inherit does. Semgrep flags secrets: inherit, so the line carries an inline suppression:

    secrets: inherit  # nosemgrep: yaml.github-actions.security.secrets-inherit.secrets-inherit

docs.title: Version-agnostic evidence gates
docs.text:
Branch protection requires stable, version-agnostic aggregate checks, not per-version legs. For each matrixed kind — audit, quality, and tests — the required check is the <kind> / evidence aggregate the reusable workflow emits (audit / evidence, quality / evidence, test / evidence), never the individual … / 3.12, … / 3.13 legs. Each evidence job depends on the whole matrix, so one required context covers every version.

quality / evidence also covers the quality workflow's two single-container jobs: it aggregates quality / common (the common checks), quality / custom (the repo's custom validator), and the matrixed lint and typecheck legs. It runs even when one of them fails, so any failure fails the gate. It is required in every repo's CI-gates ruleset, whatever the language; quality / common is no longer required on its own.

The custom validator (scripts/bin/validate-custom) therefore runs in PR CI as well as in local vrg-validate, and a failing validator blocks the merge. A repo with no custom validator gets a passing no-op quality / custom job.

Because the required-check names carry no version, a matrix change merges through the normal gate — including a matrix reduction. This closes the old deadlock, where branch protection required a per-version leg that a reduced matrix could never produce, leaving the PR "expected, never reported" and permanently blocked with no --admin escape. A version change is now an ordinary PR.

The non-matrixed checks (the security scanners, the version-bump gate, the docs build) keep their fixed, version-free names, and they are required too — there are no report-only PR gates.

docs.title: [ci].primary-version for single-container jobs
docs.text: Some jobs are not matrixed — they run once in a single container (for example the security scan, the version-bump gate, and the docs build). These run on the primary version: [ci].primary-version if it is set, otherwise the newest resolved version (for Python, 3.15 today). primary-version is the escape hatch for the rare case where the newest version is not the right single-container default.

docs.title: Release packaging
docs.text:
A repo whose vergil.toml has a [package] table also builds signed .deb / .rpm packages and publishes them to the org's package repository. Three vergil-actions reusable workflows carry it; repos without [package] call none of the packaging jobs and see no change.

  • ci-package.yml (PR CI). Builds every package and install-tests it in a clean container of each target OS, rolling up into the single package / evidence gate. It runs one of two tiers: full (every build cell and every test cell) for release PRs into main and non-PR events, and reduced (every build cell, but only one test cell per format — the oldest release, on amd64) for other feature PRs.
  • cd-release.yml (release). package-matrix resolves the cells, package-build builds them unsigned, and package-sign — in the main-only package-signing environment — signs every .rpm and attests every artifact. The release job then attaches the signed packages and packages-manifest.json to the GitHub Release and dispatches to packages. Any packaging failure stops the release before it is tagged.
  • publish-index.yml (the packages repo). Rebuilds the apt and dnf index from the product releases. Before indexing anything it verifies every asset's build attestation, pinned to cd-release.yml on refs/heads/main, and every .rpm's signature, then signs the metadata in the develop-only index-signing environment and deploys to GitHub Pages.

The release caller needs secrets: inherit (see Thin-caller ci.yml). The full mechanics are in vergil-tooling's CI Architecture guide and the Package Config Reference.

docs.title: Nightly governance (ops.yml)
docs.text:
Checking this model across the fleet is itself automated. Every managed repo carries an ops.yml workflow that calls the vergil-actions reusable workflow ops-github-config.yml on a nightly schedule. A repo whose ops.yml is missing or has no schedule is treated as non-compliant. The nightly run has three jobs in every repo, and a fourth in the org's own .github repository:

  • Config audit. vrg-github-repo-config audit compares the repo's GitHub configuration and its checked-in files against the canonical Vergil configuration. It reports drift, such as branch protection that does not match the derived required-check set or a required context that no workflow can produce, and any drift fails the run. The nightly job only audits; it never changes the configuration. Reconciling a repo (apply) is a human action. See the GitHub Config Audit reference.
  • Dependabot audit. vrg-dependabot-audit fails the run when the repo has any open Dependabot alert, described below.
  • Branch sweep. vrg-branch-sweep deletes branches whose pull-request work is finished. It is the safety net behind the delete-on-merge and delete-on-close rules. See the vrg-branch-sweep reference.
  • Trusted-authors check (.github only). vrg-trusted-authors check reads back the org's published copy of the trusted-authors configuration, the Actions variables its jobs judge content against, and fails the run when one is missing, invalid, not visible to every repo, or shadowed by a repository-level copy. The daily hoshin review compares the values it read with the host configuration. One run covers the whole org, so every other repo skips the job. See vergil-actions' trusted-authors-check.

The nightly ops.yml in vergil-containers also runs the language lifecycle job, which keeps the version window current. For Python, Go, Rust and TypeScript it opens one pull request per change: an add, a drop, or (for Python) a runtime change that records a newly published vergil-python runtime. Each add or drop pull request carries its own toolchain pin change: an add writes the new series' pin and a drop removes the pin it leaves unused, so the pull request passes CI as opened. For the other languages it opens an issue instead. It never enables auto-merge: a person reviews and merges every lifecycle pull request.

The nightly ops.yml in vergil-containers and vergil-python also runs the upstream refresh, the one nightly job whose pull request merges itself. It runs as two jobs. The prepare job runs the repo's [upstream-refresh].hook with no secrets and a read-only token. The publish job checks the resulting patch against the repo's path fence, the [upstream-refresh].paths allowlist, then opens a pull request on a new automation/upstream-refresh/<run-id> branch as the org automation App. The pull request merges itself once its CI passes, and the run is red unless it merged or there was nothing to change. See vergil-tooling's upstream-refresh reference and vergil-actions' ops-upstream-refresh workflow.

docs.title: Report-only Dependabot
docs.text:
Dependabot alerts are on for every repo, and Dependabot never opens a pull request. The config audit enforces both settings: alerts on, Dependabot security updates off. Every repo also carries a canonical .github/dependabot.yml in which every entry sets open-pull-requests-limit: 0. vrg-validate rejects an entry without that limit, and the config audit flags a missing or non-canonical file. The file exists so that the OpenSSF Scorecard Dependency-Update-Tool check passes.

The nightly dependabot-audit job fails on any open alert, at any severity. vrg-dependabot-audit exits 1 when the repo has open alerts and 2 when it could not check them, and both fail the run. The log shows alert counts only. The only way to clear an alert is to fix the dependency or dismiss the alert on GitHub; nothing in the repo can suppress one.

This gate is defense in depth, aimed at dormant repos. The dependency update at release time and the language audits that run on every change remain the main dependency hygiene. See the Dependabot Alert Audit reference.

docs.title: Python toolchain selection
docs.text:
Vergil owns which Python interpreter runs. A repo's own files may declare only a floor, such as requires-python:

  • .python-version is an error. It chooses the interpreter version behind Vergil's back, so validation fails until it is deleted.
  • uv's python-preference and python-downloads are allowed. They choose where an interpreter comes from, not which version it is.
  • Vergil sets the interpreter itself. Wherever it runs Python, it sets UV_PYTHON to the resolved version and UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE=only-system, so uv always uses the image's interpreter.

See rule 13 of the Language version lifecycle and vergil-tooling's Container Config Reference.

docs.title: Rust toolchain selection
docs.text:
Vergil owns which Rust toolchain runs, as it does for Python. A repo deals only in x.y and never names a patch release:

  • A repo declares only a floor. It sets an x.y floor through rust-version in its root Cargo.toml. vrg-validate warns when the floor is below the version window's oldest series.
  • A toolchain file is an error. A rust-toolchain.toml, or the legacy rust-toolchain, chooses the toolchain behind Vergil's back, so validation fails until it is deleted.
  • The image sets the toolchain itself. Each Vergil Rust image sets RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN to its own installed release and turns rustup's auto-install off, so no repo file or setting selects another toolchain and rustup never downloads one. vrg-container-run never forwards RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN or RUSTUP_AUTO_INSTALL from the host, even when the repo's [container].env-prefixes match them.
  • CI checks the result. Each Rust CI leg asserts that rustc reports the x.y that CI resolved for it, and a mismatch fails the leg.

See the Toolchain Selection section of vergil-tooling's Rust standards and vergil-containers' Rust support policy.

docs.title: TypeScript toolchain selection
docs.text:
Vergil owns which Node runs, as it does for Python and Rust. Each Vergil TypeScript image carries one Node major, with the npm bundled with it:

  • A repo declares at most a range. It may set an engines.node range in its root package.json, and the range should admit every major in the version window. vrg-validate warns when the range admits a major below the window's oldest, or excludes the window's newest.
  • A Node or package-manager version setting is an error. A .nvmrc or .node-version file, and in the root package.json a packageManager or volta field, an npm, pnpm or yarn key under engines, or a runtime or packageManager entry under devEngines, chooses the version behind Vergil's back, so validation fails until it is removed.
  • The host's Node settings stay on the host. vrg-container-run never forwards NODE_OPTIONS, or any variable whose name starts npm_config_, COREPACK_ or VOLTA_ in any case, even when the repo's [container].env-prefixes match them.
  • CI checks the result. Each TypeScript CI leg asserts that the Node on its PATH is the major that CI resolved for it, and a mismatch fails the leg.

See the Toolchain Selection section of vergil-tooling's TypeScript standards, its Container Config Reference and vergil-containers' TypeScript / Node.js support policy.

docs.title: Supported languages
docs.text:
Vergil supports a set of first-class languages under one shared model: containerized, multi-version toolchains with a common validation pipeline (lint, typecheck, test + coverage, dependency audit). Each language is added the same way — a registry entry, a strictness policy, prebuilt container images, and reusable CI — so every repository is validated identically regardless of the language it is written in. Each language's versions come from its version window, published by vergil-containers and derived from the upstream community's release and end-of-life policy, not from workflow code; see vergil-containers' Language version lifecycle for the per-language policies, and Continuous integration for the fleet-wide, version-agnostic CI model.

This page is the fleet-level summary. The authoritative, per-language standards (toolchains, strictness rules, naming, testing and coverage) live in vergil-tooling and are linked below rather than restated here.

Language Standards Python Python standards Go Go standards Rust Rust standards C++ C++ standards TypeScript (new) TypeScript standards

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text:
TypeScript is the newest first-class language, and the first new language added since the extension model matured with C++. It follows the same containerized, multi-version pattern as the rest of the fleet. The v1 shape:

  • Node.js runtime, single canonical tsc. TypeScript has no Clang-vs-GCC analog — there is exactly one typechecker. So TYPECHECK, LINT, and AUDIT each run once, and only the test stage fans out per Node major. That makes the expensive matrix axis the Node version, not the compiler — and makes TypeScript lighter on merge gates than C++.
  • Multi-version container images. The toolchain ships as prebuilt stable images for the supported Node majors — node-26 (primary), node-24 and node-22 — never built from source.
  • npm for install and audit. Install is npm ci (a clean, lockfile-pinned install from package-lock.json); the dependency audit is npm audit. npm was chosen for universality at zero adoption barrier.
  • Warnings to 11, via a shareable strict base tsconfig. Strictness is the baseline, not a luxury: consumers extend a shared strict base tsconfig (strict plus a curated set of extras promoted to errors), so every repository typechecks clean against the same rules.
  • 100% coverage with Vitest + V8. The house line is held at 100% via Vitest's V8 coverage, with explicit /* v8 ignore */ markers as the acknowledged-gap valve — gaps are declared, never silently dropped.
  • ESM-first. v1 targets native ES modules (nodenext resolution, es2022 target); CommonJS and plain untyped JavaScript are out of scope for v1.

For the full toolchain, strictness rules, and testing policy, see the TypeScript standards in vergil-tooling:

  • Toolchain and strictness
  • Testing and coverage
  • Naming conventions

docs.title: Package repository
docs.text:
Vergil products are published as signed OS packages — .deb for Ubuntu and .rpm for RHEL — through one org-wide package repository. This page is the fleet-level summary. The full install commands live in the packages README, and the build side lives in vergil-tooling's Package Config Reference and CI Architecture guide.

The packages are built, signed, published and install-tested for consumers outside Vergil. Vergil itself does not install from them: every Vergil install of vergil-tooling uses uv from git (see Who installs which way).

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
The repository is served from GitHub Pages at https://vergil-project.github.io/packages:

Format Path Releases apt /deb Ubuntu 24.04 (noble), Ubuntu 26.04 (resolute) rpm /rpm/el9, /rpm/el10 RHEL 9, RHEL 10

Every release is published for both amd64 and arm64. The indexed products today are vergil-tooling, vergil-python (the pinned CPython runtime the Python products run on), and vergil-archive-keyring (built by the packages repo itself).

docs.title: Bootstrapping a host
docs.text:
A host trusts the repository in four steps:

  1. Fetch the public key from keys/vergil.asc on the repository site.
  2. Verify that it holds exactly one primary key, with fingerprint B3A1D804DC03AB036566A4E367861822166ECABE.
  3. Add a temporary bootstrap source signed by that key and install vergil-archive-keyring. From then on the keyring package owns the key and the permanent apt source / dnf repo file.
  4. Remove the bootstrap source and key.

The exact apt and dnf commands are in the packages README and are not repeated here. When vrg-package builds or install-tests a Python product, it performs this bootstrap itself to install the vergil-python runtime, and refuses any key whose primary fingerprint differs from the pinned one.

docs.title: Signing model
docs.text:
The org has one OpenPGP identity. Its primary key is RSA-4096, certify-only, and held offline by a human. CI never sees it. CI holds only a signing subkey, which signs every .rpm and the apt (InRelease / Release.gpg) and dnf (repomd.xml) metadata.

Trust the primary fingerprint, not the subkey. The subkey rotates: a new one is minted offline and shipped as a new vergil-archive-keyring release, so a host that trusts the primary picks it up through an ordinary upgrade.

The subkey lives in GitHub environments restricted by branch: package-signing (admits only main) in each product repo, where a release signs its packages, and index-signing (admits only develop) in packages, where the index is signed. Sigstore build-provenance attestations are an extra layer on top of the signatures, never the trust root.

docs.title: Who installs which way
docs.text:
Every Vergil install of vergil-tooling is uv tool install from git, on a uv-managed Python 3.15. A release install resolves its tag to one commit and constrains its dependencies to that commit's own uv.lock. None of them reads the package repository.

Environment How vergil-tooling is installed Agent VMs (Lima and cloud) vrg-vm resolves the identity's version to one commit with git ls-remote and installs that commit from git, constrained by its uv.lock Dev containers The per-branch cache build installs every ref from git on the image's uv-managed Python 3.15 (VERGIL_CORE_PYTHON_DIR), with interpreter downloads off; a release pin is constrained by its commit's uv.lock, a dev ref is not (see CI architecture and How the cache tracks vergil-tooling releases) CI (GitHub-hosted runners and container jobs) The vergil-actions setup action installs from git, constrained by the resolved commit's uv.lock macOS host uv tool install --no-config --python 3.15 --managed-python of the exact release tag, constrained by the tag's uv.lock; the release's install stage ([publish].install) runs it, and a first install follows vergil-tooling's Getting Started

On a VM, a version with no release tag, a failed lock export or a failed install fails provisioning: vrg-vm never falls back to another version or to an unconstrained install. VMs made before the move to uv installed vergil-tooling as an apt package. Once the uv install passes its check, vrg-vm update removes the vergil packages, the vergil apt source and its key from them, and vrg-vm create no longer sets up the package repository. See vergil-tooling's VM spec reference.

Packaged Python products depend on the vergil-python runtime series they were built against. vergil-python publishes one package per listed CPython series, vergil-python<x.y>, and every release publishes every listed series. A package's version is <cpython>+<pbs_tag>.<release>, where <release> is the vergil-python release that built it (for example 3.15.1+20261021.1.0.4); releases before v1.0.4 lack the .<release> suffix. A product depends on vergil-python<x.y> (>= <installed version>), the runtime version it was built against, so later patches and rebuilds of the same series satisfy it.

The series is derived: it is the newest window version with a published runtime. A product can instead pin an exact x.y.z with [package.python] runtime, and then the build fails if the series package serves any other patch. For a pinned product, the vergil updater in vrg-update-deps bumps the pin to the patch the series package serves, only once every package index the build and install-test read from serves it, and never outside the pin's series: a newer series is reported as held back. See vergil-tooling's Package Config Reference and Dependency Update Config.

docs.title: Publishing a product
docs.text: A repo opts in by adding a [package] table to its vergil.toml (builder, vendor, summary, smoke test, and target selection). With it present, PR CI builds and install-tests the packages, and a release builds, signs, attests and attaches them to the GitHub Release, then notifies packages to re-index. Without it, nothing changes. The keys are documented in the Package Config Reference; the pipeline is summarized under Release packaging.

docs.title: Logbook
docs.text:
Vergil does a large share of its work unattended: lifecycle and upstream-refresh PRs open and merge themselves, CD builds publish images, and scheduled and event-driven jobs run whether or not anyone is looking. The logbook is the written record of the management cadence that looks at all of it: a fixed set of reviews at the start and end of each day, and at week, month, quarter and year boundaries, run with /vergil:hoshin. Every review writes one dated entry here, even when it finds nothing, so the record proves each review ran and later reviews can read earlier ones.

  • Hoshin kanri: the method behind the reviews, and why they are shaped as they are.
  • Hoshin: the direction document, holding the fleet's vital few.
  • Fleet: the fleet roster, each org active or inactive.
  • The entries, by level: daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly and yearly.

docs.title: Time zone
docs.text:
Every date and time in the logbook is computed in this IANA time zone, never from the host clock:

Time zone: America/New_York

docs.title: File names
docs.text:
Every path is ASCII and names the period the review covers, plus the mode, start or end:

Level File name Example Daily daily/YYYY-MM-DD-<mode>.md daily/2026-11-18-start.md Weekly weekly/<Monday's YYYY-MM-DD>-<mode>.md weekly/2026-11-16-end.md Monthly monthly/YYYY-MM-<mode>.md monthly/2026-11-start.md Quarterly quarterly/YYYY-Qn-<mode>.md quarterly/2026-Q4-end.md Yearly yearly/YYYY-<mode>.md yearly/2026-start.md

Weeks run Monday to Sunday, and a week is named by its Monday's date. Every period comes from the week: a week belongs to the month its Monday falls in, and so to that month's quarter and year. The week of Monday 2025-12-29 belongs to December 2025, Q4 2025 and the year 2025.

docs.title: Entries
docs.text:
An entry is free-form Markdown under a minimal header, YAML front matter with exactly these keys:

level: daily            # daily | weekly | monthly | quarterly | yearly
mode: start             # start | end
period: 2026-11-18      # the file name's period part
window_from: 2026-11-17T18:42-05:00   # omitted on a not-performed entry
window_to: 2026-11-18T08:05-05:00     # omitted on a not-performed entry
ran_at: 2026-11-18T08:05-05:00
late: false
not_performed: false

The body is the review: what was found, what was decided, the follow-up issues filed, and the kaizen notes. A run where nothing happened still writes an entry, saying so. A "not performed" entry is a few lines: that the review was not done, and the human's note on why, if any. The format is kept loose on purpose.

A run never edits an entry already merged by an earlier run. A late or "not performed" close is its own new file.

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text:
Each level's index.md lists that level's entries, newest first, under its level heading, one line per entry:

- [<period> <mode>](<file name>)

An entry that ran late or was not performed adds a space and (late) or (not performed) at the end of its line. A run adds its own entries to the indexes in the same PR as the entries.

docs.title: 方針 Hoshin
docs.text: The vital few are the fleet's three to five objectives, deliberately not a long list, each with a line on why it matters and how progress will be judged. They are set at the yearly and quarterly start reviews by キャッチボール catchball, the agent proposing and the human adjusting until both accept, and every weekly review checks the work against them. This is a current document, not a log: its history is its git history and the entries that changed it.

docs.title: Direction
docs.text: Vergil is a personal engineering toolkit: the means of building tooling and software that automates complex problems sustainably and securely, at an enterprise organization's bar for standards, security, quality and maintainability, scaled down to one person. It is a lab first, free to experiment, and a factory that produces real things. The human's time goes to designs, to breaking large undertakings into epics, and to saying "go"; the hoshin cadence is how one person steers it. The full direction is in the 2026 yearly start.

docs.title: The vital few: 2026-Q4
docs.text:
Set at the 2026-Q4 start, for the six weeks to 2027-01-04. Their shared theme: round out Vergil 2 and its management ecosystem, and prepare 2027.

Objective Why it matters How progress is judged Run the cadence Hoshin kanri keeps one person on target, and the logbook publishes the project's plans as it goes. A start entry every working day; every week closed; no stale logbook tasks. Drain the queues The backlog was grown on purpose; now one person proves they can drive the engine through it. vergil-project planning from 61 items to 20 or fewer by 2027-01-04; intake reviewed weekly to zero; every deferred item names its blocker; every open security record reviewed, the stale ones closed. Keep the fleet green Automation that cannot be trusted to stay green is not unattended. No red run or stuck automation PR older than a day without an issue and an owner. Plan 2027 The new home server arrives in February and should land on a plan. The forge migration and Vergil 3 epics through epic-create, spec and plan, by 2027-01-04.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Failed and cancelled runs. Each failure below comes from the nightly Ops schedule, or from the automation PR that schedule opened:

  • vergil-project/vergil-containers, Ops (schedule), failure: a security-related failure, vergil-project/.github#1473. The nightly image rebuild has published no new base images since 2026-11-20, and the images built on them fail with it.
  • vergil-project/vergil-containers, CI (pull request, the upstream-refresh PR vergil-project/vergil-containers#980), failure: the same security-related failure, vergil-project/.github#1473.
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux, Ops (schedule), failure: a security-related failure, logical-minds-foundry/.github#413; and the repo-config sync PR did not merge (below).
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux, CI (pull request, the repo-config sync PR logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux#1746), failure: the docs build cannot install a dependency that needs a C compiler the image lacks, tracked in logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux#1738; and a security-related failure, logical-minds-foundry/.github#413.
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability, Ops (schedule), failure: its repo-config sync PR did not merge (below).
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability, CI (pull request, logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#80), failure: the same docs-build problem, tracked in logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#72.

None of these is new: each repo's Ops run was also red the night before, the two logical-minds-foundry repos' for at least nine nights.

logical-minds-foundry: no failed runs in its private repos.

Automation PRs. None merged in the window. Four are open, and all four are stuck on failing checks:

  • vergil-project/vergil-containers#980, "chore(upstream): refresh upstream inputs", 3 hours old: a security-related failure, vergil-project/.github#1473.
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux#1746, "chore(repo-config): sync the managed files with the released templates", 5 hours old: the docs build (logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux#1738) and a security-related failure (logical-minds-foundry/.github#413).
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#80, the same sync, 5 hours old: the docs build (logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#72).
  • mnemosys-project/melete#273, the same sync, 20 hours old: its unit tests run a build command that needs npm, which the image lacks, tracked in mnemosys-project/melete#265. Its Ops run, outside this window, has been red for ten nights.

Each sync PR is closed and opened again every night, so its age resets; the failures behind them are older than the PRs show.

Releases. No releases in the window.

Security and audit signals. 2 repos across the fleet with an audit or alert signal, each a security-related failure above: vergil-project/.github#1473 and logical-minds-foundry/.github#413.

Open security records. 95 open across the fleet, the two above included. Neither signal had a record before this review; both were created in it.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Operational discipline comes before development. Monday 2026-11-23 starts by fixing the four red repos, before any new development:

  1. vergil-project/.github#1473 first, since the fleet's base images are not being rebuilt.
  2. logical-minds-foundry/.github#413.
  3. logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux#1738 and logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#72, the shared docs-build problem.
  4. mnemosys-project/melete#265.

Every failure already has an issue; what each lacked was an owner and a day: each is taken on Monday, in this order.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text:
• Recorded a security finding: vergil-project/.github#1473.
  • Recorded a security finding: logical-minds-foundry/.github#413.

docs.title: Kaizen
docs.text:
• Show how long a failure has been red. Each check compares a run only with the one before it, so a failure red for ten nights looks the same as one red since yesterday. The failed-runs and automation-PR checks should count consecutive red nights.
  • Mechanize the failed-runs check. It ran the same per-repo run list across 33 repos, then per-run and per-job log reads; a run with many jobs cannot return its failed logs in one call. It is the next candidate for a vrg-* tool (history, vergil-project/.github#1317).
  • The user identity cannot see what a security record needs. It cannot read Dependabot alerts or a run's artifacts, so one record was created without naming the package. The review needs a sanctioned way to read them.
  • Nightly sync PRs that close and reopen hide their real age; the checks should report the age of the failure, not of the PR.

docs.title: 朝礼 chōrei: daily start 2026-11-23
docs.text: The first daily review of ordinary use. Its window runs from the bootstrap chōrei's checks on Saturday morning to Monday morning, and covers 696 workflow runs across the fleet's 32 active public repos.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Failed and cancelled runs.

  • vergil-project/vergil-tooling, Epic Rollup (issues), failure, 16 runs since 2026-11-22 18:25: the rollup stops because the trusted-authors configuration does not reach the job. It began the minute vergil-project/vergil-tooling#4973 merged. vergil-tooling's own jobs run its unreleased develop, which now needs the variable, while the released reusable workflow (vergil-actions v2.1.89) does not yet pass it; vergil-project/vergil-actions#1359 does, unreleased. Epic vergil-project/.github#1467 releases it in its deployment vergil-project/.github#1487, together with the variables.
  • vergil-project/vergil-containers, Ops (schedule), failure, on both nights; CD (push), failure, on 2026-11-22; CI (pull request) on the upstream-refresh PR and on vergil-project/vergil-containers#982, failure: a security-related failure, vergil-project/.github#1473. The fix for the dev images merged (vergil-project/vergil-containers#992): the dev rebuild was green overnight and the upstream refresh merged. The prod rebuild is still blocked by it. Ops has been red four nights running.
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability, Ops (schedule), failure, on both nights: its repo-config sync PR cannot merge (below). Its CI also failed on the sync PRs and on the PR for feature/82-drop-actions-read, all on the docs build, logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#72. Ops has been red 24 nights running.
  • mnemosys-project/melete, Ops (schedule), failure, on both nights; CI (pull request) on its sync PRs, failure: the unit tests need npm, which the image lacks, mnemosys-project/melete#265. Ops has been red 23 nights running.
  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux, Ops (schedule) and CI on its sync PR, failure on 2026-11-22: the docs build and a security-related failure, logical-minds-foundry/.github#413. Now green: its sync PR merged and Monday's Ops run passed, after about ten red nights.
  • vergil-project/packages, Publish package index (repository_dispatch), failure: GitHub Pages served a stale file to the live check; the next publish passed.
  • vergil-project/vergil-tooling: six CI runs on development PRs failed, each fixed before its PR merged; one CD docs job was cancelled by a newer run.

logical-minds-foundry: no failed runs in its private repos; its only private repo is archived.

Automation PRs. Two merged in the window: vergil-project/vergil-containers#993 (upstream refresh) and logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab-for-linux#1755 (repo-config sync). Two are open, and both are stuck on failing checks:

  • logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#85, "chore(repo-config): sync the managed files with the released templates", 6 hours old: the docs build, logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#72.
  • mnemosys-project/melete#275, the same sync, 22 hours old: the unit tests, mnemosys-project/melete#265.

Releases. vergil-tooling v2.1.333, v2.1.334 and v2.1.335; vergil-actions v2.1.89; vergil-claude-plugin v2.1.84; and two releases of each of the six fixtures on 2026-11-22.

Security and audit signals. 2 repos across the fleet with an audit or alert signal, each a security-related failure above: vergil-project/.github#1473 and logical-minds-foundry/.github#413.

Open security records. 128 open across the fleet, the two above included. No finding in the window needed a new record.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Construction-phase red is accepted. While the epics in flight are finished, a red job that is a side effect of that work is accepted, and expected to clear as the epics complete; what they leave red becomes a follow-up. Strict no-red discipline starts once the fleet first reaches all-green.

  • The vergil-tooling Epic Rollup failures are such a side effect of vergil-project/.github#1467 and clear with vergil-project/.github#1487. No follow-up.

Today's failures are worked ad hoc, in a separate operations session, in this order:

  1. vergil-project/.github#1473: the prod rebuild.
  2. logical-minds-foundry/.github#413: whether the record can close now that the repo is green.
  3. logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-observability#72: the docs build.
  4. mnemosys-project/melete#265.

The operations queue replaces the hunt. Once vergil-project/.github#1494 lands, every unattended job reports its failures as issues, and this review reads that queue instead of searching run history.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text: • vergil-project/vergil-tooling#5001: allow the read-only git and gh queries the wrappers block.

docs.title: Kaizen
docs.text:
• Read-only wrapper gaps are fixed in the wrappers. The preflight's origin check and three other read-only queries were refused by the wrappers. The rule is to extend the wrapper, not to work around it (vergil-project/vergil-tooling#5001).
  • Count consecutive red nights in the failed-runs check. This review counted them by hand, per repo, from the Ops run history.
  • A run with many jobs needs its failed log read per job. Reading the whole run's failed log fails on the API limit; the check's queries should say so.
  • Trace unreleased work to its release. Finding why vergil-actions was unreleased meant reading its unreleased PRs, their tasks, the epic's plan and its deployment tasks by hand: a candidate vrg-* tool that reports, per repo, what is unreleased and which deployment task releases it.
  • Explain the open-records count. 128 open security records, up from 95, is noise unless the check says what changed.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
The vital few were set for the first time, by catchball, from the yearly start's objectives for the rest of 2026; they are now in hoshin.md:

  1. Run the cadence.
  2. Drain the queues (vergil-project's, for Q4).
  3. Keep the fleet green.
  4. Plan 2027.

The capacity plan:

  1. Capacity: about 10 epics a week, so roughly 60 in the six weeks to 2027-01-04 if the pace holds; the pace is rising.
  2. Finish first: vergil-project/.github#1384, the accelerator, then vergil-project/.github#1318 and vergil-project/.github#1440. vergil-project/.github#1374, vergil-project/.github#375 and vergil-project/.github#388 advance as they fit.
  3. The planning burn-down: two or three small or medium items a day, 10 to 15 a week, enough to reach 20 or fewer net of new inflow. The risk is inflow: 42 intake items arrived in four days. Large and extra-large items wait unless they make planning itself faster.
  4. December: brainstorm the forge migration and Vergil 3 through epic-create.
  5. Security records: one cleanup pass first, closing the stale records; vergil-project/.github#724 (hardening the security-records model) waits until the cleanup shows what is live.
  6. Does not fit this quarter: the logical-minds-foundry backlog. Its intake gets one epic-review pass, deferring the MQ items with the blocker that MQ work resumes once Vergil 2 is rounded out.

  • The queue checks should report a missing queue epic as a finding rather than an error, as mnemosys-project's planning and deferred queues showed.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
The week's theme is raising the rate of work: first seeing what is going on, then finishing the three large epics in flight, then lightening planning for the small end of the queue. The planning space is still unsettled, and this focus will be refined as the cadence matures; the pace on the larger epics is revisited in a couple of weeks.

Focus:

  • Keep the fleet green: deliver vergil-project/.github#1494, the operations queue, so every unattended job reports its failures as issues and the daily review works from that queue. Getting to green starts with seeing what is red.
  • Drain the queues: finish vergil-project/.github#1467 and vergil-project/.github#1476, clearing the way for vergil-project/.github#1384, agents submitting and finalizing their own PRs, as the next large epic: it lets epic-create run far more autonomously.
  • Drain the queues: take vergil-project/.github#1273, a scaled-down epic-create for small, low-risk work, through planning. Large, high-risk changes keep their several pushback and alignment rounds on purpose, since that depth is why epics implement with few changes; the lighter path is for the small end of the planning queue.
