docs.title: Yearly
docs.text:
The yearly start review sets the three-to-five-year direction and the year's breakthrough objectives, and its end review is the 社長診断 shachō shindan, the president's diagnosis of the year as a whole.

  • 2026 start

docs.title: Yearly start 2026
docs.text: The first yearly review, run as part of the logbook's bootstrap. The 2026 year began on Monday 2026-01-05 and ends on Monday 2027-01-04, so this entry sets a lasting direction and only the last six weeks of the year's objectives; the 2027 yearly start reads it and sets the next year.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
No earlier logbook entries exist: this is the first run.

The fleet's shape, as it stands now:

Org Status Public repos Private repos Archived vergil-project active 15 0 0 logical-minds-foundry active 4 2 0 mnemosys-project active 3 0 0 mq-rest-admin-project inactive 9 0 3 diogenes-project inactive 2 0 0 vergils-nemesis inactive 1 0 0

The public repos' primary languages: 15 Shell, 11 Python, 3 Rust, 2 TypeScript, 1 Go, 1 Java and 1 Ruby (the Java, the Ruby and one Shell repo archived).

How the fleet grew in 2026:

  • January to February: mq-rest-admin-project, one library built in several languages, which needed shared validation across all of them.
  • January to March: the core Vergil repos, vergil-actions, vergil-tooling, vergil-claude-plugin and vergil-containers.
  • May to June: the org .github (the planning home), vergil-vm and the docs site.
  • June to August: the projects the toolkit serves, in logical-minds-foundry (the MQ lab) and mnemosys-project (melete).
  • October to November: vergil-python, the signed packages repository, and six language fixture repos that prove each release.

The pace is still rising. Commits to the planning repo went from 6 in September to 61 in October and 125 in the first three weeks of November. About 35 epics closed in November alone.

Open epics: 7 in vergil-project (the largest are vergil-project/.github#1384, agents submit and finalize their own PRs, 1 of 59 tasks done; vergil-project/.github#1374, agent review against cited coding standards, 1 of 28; and vergil-project/.github#1440, resumable releases, 10 of 31), 17 in logical-minds-foundry and 1 in mnemosys-project.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
The three-to-five-year direction:

Vergil is my personal engineering toolkit, my Jarvis: the means by which I do what I did for large enterprises, building tooling and software that automates complex problems sustainably and securely, scaled down to one person without lowering the bar on standards, security, quality or maintainability. It is a lab first: free to experiment, borrowable by anyone, built for no one else. It is also a factory that produces real things. My time goes to brainstorming designs, breaking large undertakings into collections of epics, and saying "go"; large pieces then get built with minimal intervention. The hoshin cadence, daily through yearly, is how one person steers that factory.

The rest of 2026: round out Vergil 2 and its management ecosystem, and prepare 2027. Every remaining item counts as rounding out Vergil 2. The biggest accelerator is vergil-project/.github#1384, agents submitting and merging their own PRs into develop, which removes the main human blocker. Releases stay with the human for now; agents gain more autonomy as better logging and auditing earn confidence. The backlog burn-down began this week, at two or three small or medium planning items a day. Large items come in only when they make planning itself faster.

The year's breakthrough objectives, for the six weeks left:

  1. The management cadence runs: hoshin every working day, and every period closed.
  2. The queues get under control: planning and deferred burned down; intake moving quickly through planning, epic-create and epic-implement; items deferred only when blocked, never for lack of time.
  3. The fleet stays green: every red run gets an issue and an owner within a day.
  4. 2027 is planned before it starts: the forge migration and Vergil 3 specified before the new home server arrives in February.

2027, previewed for the 2027 yearly start to set:

  • Off GitHub, early in the year: a self-hosted Forgejo on a dedicated home server, the foundation of a home enterprise platform, with as much of the core moved onto it as possible.
  • Vergil 3: most of the Python ported to Rust, for performance and security, and the design revisited with what Vergil 2 taught.
  • The MQ lab, finished: the showcase for what this tooling makes possible, published as a lab anyone can download.
  • The writing pipeline: reviving The Infrastructure Mindset and its queue of article ideas, and possibly an old personal website.
  • The MIMIR adversary, medium to low priority: a second workstation that seeks out the seams and security holes in the architecture.
  • The toolkit applied to the other projects as time allows; melete stays a lifelong hobby project with no deadline.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Kaizen
docs.text:
• The bootstrap should run top-down, the yearly review first, and the daily last: direction set before the day's operations were judged worked better here than the skill's fixed order.
  • The yearly review needs the fleet's history, not only a snapshot. A fleet-history check (repo creation dates, epics closed per month) would replace several ad hoc queries.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Vergil's Management layer is how work is organized and moved — from a raw idea to a merged, closed change — across every repository and org in the fleet. It is one of several Vergil frameworks (alongside Security, Testing, and the VM/identity and container layers); this one owns the work itself: what we are doing, why, in what order, and how it gets done.

It is deliberately two-directional. Looking down, it lets you manage and zoom into the smallest unit — a single task, one pull request. Looking up, it lets you zoom out to the strategic view — every cross-cutting initiative in flight, across the whole organization, in one place. The same model serves both, and the point is to keep climbing: once you can manage tasks, you manage epics; once you can manage epics, you manage how epics interrelate.

docs.title: Units of work and delivery
docs.text:
Two definitions do the load-bearing work here:

  • The unit of work is the task — an issue that represents a single task, implemented by a single pull request and closed the moment that PR merges. This one-issue-to-one-PR discipline is exactly what makes the trailing end of the process — closing and roll-up — automatable.
  • The unit of delivery is the epic — a collection of related tasks that together implement a larger, more complex body of functionality. You deliver epics; the tasks are the to-dos that implement them.

Historically the unit was the issue: have an idea, file an issue, go do it. That broke down — a single issue was often complex enough to need many pull requests, sometimes across repositories. Splitting work from delivery fixes it: the task is small and mechanical, the epic is the meaningful whole.

docs.title: Three invariants
docs.text:
Everything in this layer follows from three rules:

  1. Every issue belongs to an epic. An issue is either an epic (or one of the bookkeeping kinds: a per-quarter archive bucket, a release tracking issue) or it has an epic parent. There is no "unlinked" state — even a one-line idea is captured under the intake epic — and the parent is the issue's state: intake, planning, deferred, or ready to build.
  2. All epics live in the organization's .github repository — one place to see every initiative in the org.
  3. Every other repository holds nothing but single-PR tasks — each closed by exactly one pull request in that same repository.

The load-bearing principle behind the third rule is task↔PR locality: a task lives in the repository whose pull request closes it. Cohesion between a task and the change that completes it matters more than a pristine issue list. In practice the .github list reads as "epics, and the issues linked under them" — you filter by the epic label for the initiatives — and the items that live there (queue items under the intake, planning and deferred epics, and the rare task whose PR edits .github itself) are linked like everything else.

docs.title: The shape of the model
docs.text:
• Epics & tasks — finite epics (in .github), plus one perpetual ad-hoc epic per repository for the small, unplanned work that should never accrete into a larger initiative.
  • Intake, planning & deferred — three standing queues that catch raw input the moment it occurs and hold it until it is ready: work flows intake → planning → ready, an evaluated item that cannot move yet waits in deferred with the conditions that will bring it back, and only ready work can be built, so nothing is lost before it is planned.
  • Workflow — how an idea becomes an epic becomes shipped tasks: the epic-create orchestrator and a front-loaded design pipeline with human-gated review rounds that makes implementation near-bulletproof.
  • Tools & skills — how the vrg-* commands and the skills fit together: what each does at the story level, and which are driven by a human versus an agent. The per-command reference lives in the repositories where the code does.
  • Hoshin kanri — the management cadence: reviews at the start and end of each day and at week, month, quarter and year boundaries, modelled on 方針管理 hōshin kanri and recorded in the logbook.

One convention is worth stating up front, because it shapes the whole lifecycle: an epic opens with a documentation task and does not close until you have reviewed it, decided what comes next, and confirmed the docs reflect what changed. Nothing is ever "done" without asking what comes next.

docs.title: Epics & tasks
docs.text: The model has exactly two artifacts — the task (the unit of work) and the epic (the unit of delivery) — plus a family of perpetual standing epics for the work that is not (or not yet) part of a plan.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A task is an issue that represents a single, self-contained change:

  • It is implemented by exactly one pull request, in the repository where that PR lands (task↔PR locality).
  • It is born linked to an epic — as is every issue: see Every issue belongs to an epic. On GitHub the link is a native sub-issue; on forges without sub-issues it degrades to a portable Parent: <owner>/<repo>#<n> line in the task body. Either way, the tooling speaks one vocabulary and never the underlying mechanism.
  • It closes when its PR merges. A task with an epic parent links its PR with the Closes keyword, so the merge closes the task automatically; the one close keyword is Closes (Fixes/Resolves are banned to keep it unambiguous).

Because a task is exactly one PR, "done" is unambiguous: once the change is in the trunk, the task is finished. Any later change is a new task, never a reopening.

Several small tasks of one epic in one repository may share a batch PR: up to 8 of them (4 by default) on one branch, each still its own commit and its own Closes line. The batch PR is rebase-merged, not squashed, so each task keeps its own commit and changelog entry on the trunk and still closes when the PR merges. A single-task PR is squash-merged as before. The worktree convention names a batch's worktree and branch.

docs.title: Finite epics
docs.text:
A finite epic is a cross-cutting initiative with an end — a real project made of related tasks, often spanning several repositories. It carries the epic label and lives in the org's .github. Its spec and plan live beside it, at epics/<n>-<slug>/ in .github.

When every child task of a finite epic is closed, the epic rolls up — it auto-closes. Roll-up is event-driven: an on: issues.closed Action fires the check on every issue close, so an epic wraps itself up the moment its last task lands, with no human bookkeeping.

docs.title: Ad-hoc epics
docs.text:
Not all work belongs to an initiative. The small, unplanned, standalone things — fix a typo in a man page, bump a pin — would clutter the model if each demanded its own epic. So every repository has exactly one ad-hoc epic: Epic (ad hoc): <repo>, labelled epic + ad-hoc, and (like all epics) located in .github. Its tasks live in the target repository, linked across.

An ad-hoc epic holds standalone work only: each of its tasks can be picked up, merged and released on its own. A task owned by another epic or by a skill never goes there. A task of another org's epic goes under that epic's proxy, and the Logbook: tasks that /vergil:hoshin files go under the hoshin epic. No filing-time guard enforces this: vrg-epic-audit reports an open ad-hoc task that looks misplaced (a Logbook: title, or a body naming an epic in another org) for a human to rule on, and a trusted Standalone-confirmed comment on a task ruled standalone stops the report.

ad-hoc is the single marker for this perpetual variant. An earlier standing alias has been retired — removed from the code and the label registry — so ad-hoc is the only form the model recognises.

An ad-hoc epic is perpetual: created once, never auto-closed, kept open even when empty, and it holds only work that stands alone. The name does deliberate work — "ad hoc" is the smell a serious engineer drives toward zero. The long-term goal is for ad-hoc work to become the rare exception as real work is increasingly shaped into finite, tidy, self-closing epics.

As its children close they drain into per-quarter archive buckets, so the live ad-hoc epic shows only work still in flight.

Ready ad-hoc tasks are worked with epic-implement in its adhoc mode, which collects them across every ad-hoc epic with vrg-queue adhoc and proposes one strategy for the human to confirm; see Working the ad-hoc tasks.

docs.title: Standing epics
docs.text:
The ad-hoc epic is one of five standing epics — perpetual umbrellas that are created once, reused, and never roll up:

Standing epic Holds Epic (ad hoc): <repo> ready one-off work for one repository Epic (intake): <name> captured, unreviewed items — and every orphan the sweep finds Epic (planning): <name> items waiting for (or undergoing) epic creation Epic (deferred): <name> evaluated items parked until their revival conditions are met Epic (hoshin): <org> the Logbook: tasks that /vergil:hoshin files and works

There is one ad-hoc epic per repository. The intake, planning and deferred epics come as a set per queue home: the org's .github, shared by every repository in the org. They are the three queues that hold work before it is ready to build — see Intake, planning & deferred.

There is one hoshin epic per org, labelled epic + hoshin. It is always homed in <org>/.github. It is not a queue: its tasks are ready to build, but only /vergil:hoshin (the hoshin kanri review cadence) files and works them, so no queue review or ad-hoc run picks them up, and no intake route moves an item into it. Its closed children drain into per-quarter archives like the other standing epics'.

docs.title: Proxy epics
docs.text:
A development epic's work sometimes lands in a repository of another org. A proxy epic is the same-org umbrella for those tasks: titled Epic (proxy): <owner>/<repo>#<N> — <primary's title without "Epic: "> (the primary's full ref, then its title), labelled epic + proxy, and homed in that org's .github. The development epic it serves is its primary. The link runs both ways: the proxy's body carries one Primary: <owner>/<repo>#<N> line, and the primary records each proxy in a trusted comment carrying a Proxy: <owner>/.github#<N> line. vrg-epic-create --proxy-for <primary ref> --repo <owner>/<repo> finds, reopens or creates the proxy, with its Proxy: comment on the primary.

A proxy is not a development epic. It has no spec, plan or bookends, since the primary carries them; the roll-up never closes it; and the roadmap does not list it. Its tasks are driven from the primary: epic-implement on the primary works them beside the primary's own, and refuses the proxy itself. The proxy's own org closes it: the daily sweep closes a proxy once its primary is closed and it has no open task. vrg-epic-audit --epic reports a Primary: / Proxy: link where the two sides disagree.

docs.title: Epic categories
docs.text:
Every epic carries exactly one category label, so one label filter in the GitHub UI shows each category:

Category Epics Category label Development every finite epic: planned with epic-create, closed by roll-up epic-development Management the intake, planning, deferred and hoshin standing epics epic-management Ad hoc each repository's ad-hoc epic ad-hoc Proxy each proxy epic proxy

ad-hoc and proxy are both the marker the tools read and the category label. epic-development and epic-management are new, and they are for display only: no tool reads either of them to decide behaviour or to find an epic. An archive bucket is not an epic and has no category.

The tools apply the category label when they create an epic. vrg-epic-create derives it from the epic's other labels, and refuses, creating nothing, a caller-given epic-development or epic-management label and labels that mark two categories at once (for example ad-hoc and proxy). The path that creates a standing epic on demand adds epic-management to a new intake, planning, deferred or hoshin epic.

Epics created before the category labels existed are labelled once, by the one-off deployment vergil-project/.github#1460. vrg-ensure-label --repo <owner>/<repo> --label <name> creates one registered label from the label registry.

docs.title: Every issue belongs to an epic
docs.text:
In any managed repository, every issue is either a legitimate top-level kind or has an epic parent. The top-level kinds are epics (including the standing ones), the per-quarter archive buckets, and the release tracking issue a release opens for its duration. Everything else — tasks, operational tasks, intake, planning and deferred items — hangs under an epic.

There is no opt-out and no "unlinked" state, and the parent is not just bookkeeping: it is the issue's state. Under the intake epic it has been captured; under the planning epic it awaits a design; under the deferred epic it waits for its revival conditions; under an ad-hoc, finite or proxy epic it is ready to build. The sanctioned tools create every issue already linked, and an issue born outside them is healed, not rejected — the daily sweep attaches it to its home's intake epic, unless an outsider opened it. An outsider's issue is never attached: it is reported, metadata only (see Trusted content).

docs.title: The bookend convention
docs.text:
An epic is never truly "done" the instant its implementation lands, because almost no real problem is 100% closed by a single initiative. So every epic carries bookend tasks:

  • It opens with a documentation task — the spec and plan, born from planning.
  • It closes with two tasks, in order: a documentation review (confirm the change is reflected in the docs — especially this site) and then the retrospective, the terminal gate — a single backward-looking record that partners the spec and plan and records what comes next. Its docs PR closes the epic.
  • A follow-on brainstorm is seeded up front only when a known follow-on already exists; otherwise its outcome is captured in the retrospective.

This rides the roll-up: because the epic cannot close until all its tasks close, the closing bookends gate completion. You cannot finish an epic without answering "now what?" and confirming the story is documented. Nothing is ever done without asking what comes next.

docs.title: Trusted content
docs.text:
The tools and skills act only on content they can trust. A body, comment, review or title counts only when an identity with a role wrote it and every identity that edited it holds one too. There are three roles: the human and the agent Apps, trusted in every Vergil org, and each org's automation App, trusted only in its own org's repositories. Content that anyone else wrote or edited is never acted on: it is reported as metadata only (the item, the account and the time), never its text. A task whose body is not trusted stops for the human instead of being worked.

Agents read issue and PR content through vrg-issue-read, the trusted read command, which prints only what the trust rule accepts; the hook guard refuses their raw content reads. Two checks keep watch, and the daily hoshin review shows both: the outsider report (vrg-epic-audit --untrusted), which lists what accounts outside the roles did in each Vergil org, and the nightly trusted-authors check, which checks each org's published copy of the configuration (see Nightly governance).

The roles are configured once, on the human's host, and published to each org for its GitHub Actions jobs. The configuration is described in vergil-tooling's Trusted authors section, and the order in which to publish it in vergil-actions' VRG_TRUSTED_AUTHORS section.

docs.title: Compliance invariants
docs.text:
These guarantees are enforced, not just documented. vrg-epic-audit is a read-only sweep (with a human-gated --close) that flags drift and invariant violations:

  • Epics live in .github. Every repository's epics belong in the org's .github; an epic that has leaked out is flagged.
  • No stray .github issues. The epic home holds only epics, the per-quarter archive buckets, and issues linked under an epic — tasks and intake, planning and deferred queue items alike. Any other open issue there is a stray.
  • An epic is never closed while a child is open. Roll-up closes a finite epic only once all its children are closed; a closed epic with a still-open child is a violation, remediated by reopening it. (Standing epics never roll up; their closed children drain into archives instead.)
  • Every issue has an epic parent. An orphan — an open issue that is neither a top-level kind nor linked under an epic — is reported, along with any issue still carrying the retired triage / idea / research labels.

The daily sweep (vrg-epic-audit --close) does more than report: its orphan pass auto-heals the model. It converts body-only parent links into native ones, strips the retired labels, and attaches every orphan to its home's intake epic, except one an outsider opened, which it reports instead. It never closes an item, and it stops loudly — never silently skipping — when a queue is too full to accept more.

The sweep does not run the security-records pass: vrg-epic-audit --close makes no security-advisory call. The pass is vrg-security-record sync, which the human or the user agent runs over the private draft advisories in the org's .github; nothing runs it on a schedule, and the read-only vrg-epic-audit only previews it. Each advisory follows the neutral security issues it tracks: closed once every one of them is closed as completed and none is a queue item, a draft while any is open. The close guard keeps an advisory draft, reported on a held: line, while any issue it tracks is a queue item (live or archived) or was closed with a reason other than completed; retarget it to the task that fixes it, or close it with vrg-security-record close and a reason. Broken pairs are reported for a human to resolve, never repaired. See vergil-tooling's Security Records guide.

When a finite epic is found outside its home, relocate it: move the issue into .github with vrg-gh issue transfer, then re-establish its task links with vrg-epic-link.

The exact rules and commands are in vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards.

docs.title: Hoshin kanri
docs.text:
Vergil does a large share of its work unattended, and the faster development goes, the more the small instabilities in that work show. The fast, ad hoc engineering work needs a management cadence beside it: a fixed set of reviews at the start and end of each day, and at week, month, quarter and year boundaries, each leaving a written record in the logbook. This page explains the model those reviews follow, so a later reader understands why they are shaped as they are.

The decision behind it: until a better framework is found, Vergil scales 方針管理 hōshin kanri down to one person working with agents, and adopts its practices in spirit where not to the letter. The skill, its documents and the logbook use the method's Japanese terms freely, in content. Vergil is a personal, single-user stack that takes no outside contributions, so the vocabulary is chosen for its one reader.

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
The word. 方針 hōshin is policy or direction; the characters are literally "direction" and "needle", as in a compass needle. 管理 kanri is management. In English it is usually called policy deployment.

Origin. It grew out of Japan's total quality control movement in the late 1950s and 1960s, building on Deming's plan–do–check–act cycle and Drucker's management by objectives. Bridgestone Tire is usually credited with naming and first using it in 1965 (one history dates the company's idea to systematize it to 1962); Komatsu and Toyota were early adopters. Hewlett-Packard brought it to the US in the 1980s, and Danaher made it central to the Danaher Business System.

How it works.

  1. A three-to-five-year direction yields a small number of yearly breakthrough objectives: the vital few, deliberately not a long list.
  2. Each level turns the objectives above it into its own targets and the means of reaching them.
  3. キャッチボール catchball: targets and means pass back and forth between levels until both sides agree they are achievable. Direction comes from the top; the means are agreed with the people doing the work.
  4. Two halves: hōshin, which drives change toward the direction, and 日常管理 nichijō kanri (daily management), which keeps normal operation stable and standardised. Hōshin assumes daily management is under control.
  5. A nested review cadence (monthly, quarterly), and a yearly review by top management, 社長診断 shachō shindan (the president's diagnosis). Each review's findings feed the next cycle's plan.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text: Term In Vergil 方針管理 hōshin kanri The whole system; the skill is /vergil:hoshin. 日常管理 nichijō kanri The daily review, run on every invocation. 朝礼 chōrei The daily start review (morning assembly). 終礼 shūrei The daily end review (closing assembly). 方針 hōshin The direction document, hoshin.md, holding the vital few. 反省 hansei Reflection; the end review at the week, month and quarter levels. 社長診断 shachō shindan The yearly end review; in a one-person company the president is the human. キャッチボール catchball Agreeing objectives and means; the agent proposes, the human adjusts, until both accept. 改善 kaizen Notes, in each entry, on improving the reviews themselves.

docs.title: The two halves
docs.text:
• Nichijō kanri (daily) runs on every invocation. start is the 朝礼 chōrei: what ran unattended since the last review, what failed and why, and what needs action today. It also shows two trust checks, in the terminal only: the outsider report (vrg-epic-audit --untrusted), what accounts outside the trusted roles did in each Vergil org since the last daily review, and the latest nightly trusted-authors check, compared with the host configuration. end is the 終礼 shūrei: what changed today, what is waiting on the human, and a note for tomorrow's chōrei.
  • Hōshin (week, month, quarter, year) runs only at boundaries, or when the human asks to close a period with end <level>. A start review sets direction for the period; an end review is 反省 hansei, reflection on the period just finished. The yearly end is the 社長診断 shachō shindan.

Every review ends with a kaizen prompt: what should this review do differently?

docs.title: The calendar in brief
docs.text:
• One command each morning. /vergil:hoshin start works out for itself which reviews are due, closes whatever period was left open, and runs them. /vergil:hoshin end [<level>] is optional: plain end closes the day, and end week, end month, end quarter or end year closes that period and every smaller one still open beneath it.
  • One time zone. Every date and time is computed in the IANA time zone recorded in the logbook, never from the host clock.
  • Days. A day with a start entry is a day worked; a day with none is a day off, and nothing about it is flagged.
  • Weeks run Monday to Sunday, and every period comes from the week: a week belongs to the month its Monday falls in, and so to that month's quarter and year. The week of Monday 2025-12-29 belongs to December 2025, Q4 2025 and 2025, so January 2026, Q1 2026 and 2026 begin with the week of Monday 2026-01-05.
  • Order. Closing reviews run first, smallest level first, since reflection rolls up. Then the daily chōrei runs, so operations are known to be stable before direction is set, and the boundary start reviews follow from the largest level down, since direction flows top-down.
  • Nothing silently skipped. A period opened and never closed is offered for closing at the next start: run the missed end review late, or record it as not performed. At the week level and above, periods with no entries at all are named as gaps in the next start entry.
  • Windows. Each review covers a window from the end of the last reviewed window, so a skipped day widens the next window rather than losing time.
  • The first run on an empty logbook opens every level, and sets the first vital few by catchball.

docs.title: Scaled to one person and agents
docs.text:
In a company, hōshin kanri runs through layers of management, and catchball passes between them. Vergil has one person and the agents working with them, so the method is adopted in spirit where not to the letter:

  • The human is every level of management. The yearly shachō shindan is the human's own review of the year; there is no one above them to report to.
  • Catchball is between the human and the agent. The agent proposes objectives, focus and means from the durable record; the human adjusts until both accept.
  • The agent does the gathering. Each review's data comes from durable state (git and GitHub today), through vrg-* tools where they exist. Every check the skill runs by hand is written as the brief for a tool that will later do it deterministically.
  • The cadence fits the human's working day. start is run on most working days, weekends included, and carries the boundaries; end is the human's choice, because the day ends when it ends.
  • The record is public and light. The logbook is Markdown with a minimal header, published on this site, and nothing a security record keeps private appears in it.
  • Kaizen improves the reviews themselves. Each entry's kaizen notes feed back into the skill, so the first, deliberately thin checklists grow through use.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Akao, Y. (ed.), Hoshin Kanri: Policy Deployment for Successful TQM, Productivity Press, 1991 (English edition).
  • Lean Enterprise Institute lexicon, "Hoshin Kanri": https://www.lean.org/lexicon-terms/hoshin-kanri/
  • Akao's book, Appendix 1, "History of Hoshin Kanri" (2020 reissue): https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/hoshin-kanri/9781000286656/xhtml/18_Appendix01.xhtml
  • All About Lean, "The Evolution of Strategic Management — Hoshin Kanri": https://www.allaboutlean.com/evolution-of-strategic-management-hoshin-kanri/
  • Wikipedia, "Hoshin Kanri": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoshin_Kanri

The Bridgestone dates come from the Akao and All About Lean histories; the Lean Enterprise Institute and Wikipedia pages give no dates. The term 社長診断 for the yearly review is the human's own, from years of working in Japanese; English sources call it the president's diagnosis.

docs.title: Intake, planning & deferred
docs.text:
The formal path — brainstorm, spec, epic, tasks — is the preferred on-ramp, but most work does not arrive that way. It arrives as a dog-walk epiphany, a "we should probably…", an "oh, don't forget." Intake is the lossless net: it turns raw input into a tracked issue with near-zero friction, so nothing is lost before it can be planned.

Capturing the seed of an idea when it is fresh is more valuable than planning it out on the spot. Intake optimizes for that.

docs.title: Every issue belongs to an epic
docs.text:
The net is not an exception to the model — it is part of it. In every managed repository, every issue is either a legitimate top-level kind (an epic, a per-quarter archive bucket, or a release tracking issue) or has an epic parent. There is no opt-out and no "unlinked" state, and that includes a half-formed idea captured thirty seconds ago.

What makes that workable is that the parent is the state. An issue's parent epic says where it stands, so no label has to restate it:

State Parent Buildable? Intake — captured, not yet reviewed the intake epic no Planning — judged to need a full epic the planning epic no Deferred — evaluated, but waiting on something before it can move the deferred epic no Ready — a one-off, or part of a planned initiative a repository's ad-hoc epic, a finite epic, or a proxy epic yes

Work moves intake → planning → ready. An item that has been evaluated but cannot move yet — it waits on an upstream release, another issue, a date, or capacity — steps aside into the deferred queue until its revival conditions are met. Only ready work can be built: the pull-request tooling refuses an issue that still sits in the intake, planning or deferred queue, and says which step to take first.

docs.title: The standing queues
docs.text:
The three queues are standing epics — perpetual, like a repository's ad-hoc epic: created once, reused, never auto-closed. Epic (intake): <name> holds captured, unreviewed items; Epic (planning): <name> holds items waiting for (or undergoing) epic creation; Epic (deferred): <name> holds evaluated items parked until their revival conditions are met.

There is one set per queue home, the org's .github. Every repository shares it, so the whole org-wide queue is one view rather than something scattered across repositories. Closed items drain into per-quarter archive buckets, so the live queues show only open work.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Capture. The moment something is worth remembering, it becomes an intake item — filed already linked under the intake epic. A one-line "don't forget X" is valid, and there is no category to choose: a bug, a spark, and an investigation all enter the same way. No planning, no scoping; that is deliberately deferred.
  2. Review. On a periodic pass, intake is reviewed oldest first, in small batches. For each item the agent checks its current state and recommends a route; the human confirms the batch. There are five routes:
  3. Drop — close it with a reason (not planned). It stays searchable.
  4. Defer — move it into the deferred queue, recording why it waits and what to check before it can come back.
  5. One-off — move it into its target repository as a ready task under that repository's ad-hoc epic (or a named epic). The ad-hoc epic takes only standalone work: an item that is work of a development epic in another org goes under that epic's proxy in the target repository's org, never ad-hoc, and one in the primary's own org goes under the primary itself. A one-off never goes under the hoshin epic: only /vergil:hoshin files its tasks.
  6. Split — replace it with several ready tasks and close it.
  7. Planning — it needs a real design, so it moves to the planning queue, with an estimated epic size.
  8. Plan. A planning review keeps the planning queue correct, oldest first: each item is left (most are), deferred, dropped, or, unusually, sent out as a one-off, to a repository's ad-hoc epic or, for another org's epic, to its proxy, by the same rule as from intake. It never picks. The human chooses what to plan next and runs epic-create on it, picking only what will be implemented soon, since a plan left sitting goes stale. A planning item is the record of its own epic creation: epic-create always works through one, and leaves progress comments so a session can pause and resume days later. A planning item is waiting, in progress, or completed — closed as "planned as" the epic it became, or with the reason it is not worth doing.

A planning item can carry an estimated epic size: S (1–9 tasks), M (10–19), L (20–39) or XL (40+), derived from an estimated task count. Sizing is optional: an item stays unsized (? in vrg-queue) until it is sized. A size is recorded as an epic-size:<S|M|L|XL> label and a dated Sized … comment, both written by vrg-intake-route: an item is sized as it is routed to planning, and the planning review sizes any waiting item still unsized. Deferred items can carry a size too, and a one-off clears it. The size is there so the planning queue can be sorted and filtered by it: vrg-queue planning --sort size --size S lists the small items, oldest first, so small epics need not wait behind large ones. An item whose sizing is in error (!) is always listed too, whatever the filter. 4. Revisit. A deferred item is never forgotten, because every deferral records a reason and the conditions to check (Revisit when:). On a periodic deferred review, the agent actually checks each item's conditions against their real sources — a release page, an issue's state, a date — and recommends one outcome: keep it (not yet), refresh its record, revive it (back to intake, to planning, or as a one-off), or drop it. Only an item in a queue or an ad-hoc epic can be deferred; a task in a finite epic cannot, since parking one task would in effect suspend its whole epic.

A security item — the neutral issue half of a security record — is routed like any other and keeps its advisory links through every move: every advisory it names is retargeted when the item is transferred or recreated, and its one advisory is retargeted when it is split. A split of an item naming several advisories is refused, since which advisory goes to which task can't be inferred; retarget each by hand, one at a time, with vrg-security-record retarget <GHSA> --from <item> --to <task> [--to …], then split. The --to set is the complete set the advisory tracks afterwards: a --to for each task that fixes it and for every other open issue it still tracks, since retarget refuses a set that leaves one out and prints the command that would succeed. See vergil-tooling's Security Records guide.

The intake and planning queues are meant to stay drained: a growing one is a signal to review it, not a place for work to live. The deferred queue is not drained but re-checked — an item stays there exactly as long as its revival conditions are unmet.

docs.title: Nothing escapes
docs.text:
Issues created outside the sanctioned tools — in the web UI, by a script — are healed, not rejected. A daily sweep attaches every orphan it finds to its home's intake epic, so it surfaces at the next review instead of drifting unseen. The one exception is an issue an outsider opened: the sweep never attaches it, and reports it by metadata only (see Trusted content). Placement stays the reviewer's job; the sweep only guarantees that nothing is lost.

The former triage / idea / research kind labels are retired — the parent carries the state now, and the sweep strips the old labels.

docs.title: Mechanics
docs.text: The commands and their exact behavior — vrg-intake-create, vrg-intake-route, vrg-queue, the deferral record, the orphan pass, and the queue-home rules — are documented in vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards (see The deferred queue for deferring and reviving, and Viewing the queues for epic sizes) and the CLI reference.

docs.title: Tools & skills
docs.text:
The Management layer is operated through two surfaces:

  • vrg-* command-line tools — the mechanical operations (create an epic, link a task, run the audit), maintained in vergil-tooling.
  • Skills — the agent-facing workflows that compose those tools into a process (orchestrate an epic, capture intake, review the queue), maintained in the Claude Code plugin, vergil-claude-plugin.

This page explains how they fit together and who drives what. The dry, per-command reference — every flag of every tool — lives in the repositories where the code does; this is the story, not the man page. For the issue model's mechanics, see vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards.

docs.title: Who drives what
docs.text:
The dividing line is accountability. The speed limit is human comprehension, not code generation — so agents do the development, and humans own the irreversible, outward-facing steps.

Driven by the agent (runs as the user identity) Driven by the human Participating in the brainstorm; running the design-review rounds The judgment calls in the brainstorm, and the decision on each design-review finding and each further round Authoring specs and plans; implementing tasks Submitting the pull request (vrg-submit-pr), which turns GitHub auto-merge on Commits and PR preparation / hand-off Reviewing the change before submitting it: the submit is the decision to merge Read-only audits and dry-runs Settling develop once the PRs merge (vrg-finalize-pr, which the submit always runs) Filing intake, epics, tasks, links Write-gated ops: migration --apply, audit --close Implementing a dependency-update fix task Releases (vrg-release) and dependency updates (vrg-update-deps) Requesting a review decision, drafting the human's reply and reading it (vrg-ruling) Replying to a review-decision request, as themselves (vrg-ruling-reply)

An agent never merges and never opens a PR itself: it prepares the change and hands off, and a human takes it across the line.

docs.title: Authoring & structure
docs.text:
• vrg-epic-create (mint an epic in .github; with --proxy-for <primary ref> --repo <owner>/<repo> it instead finds, reopens or creates the proxy epic for a primary in another org, in the target's org .github, with its Proxy: comment on the primary)
  • vrg-adhoc-epic (ensure a repo's ad-hoc epic exists)
  • vrg-issue-create (create a task, born linked under an epic)

  • vrg-epic-link / vrg-epic-move (manage the epic↔task relationship)

  • vrg-issue-create --epic adhoc|intake|planning|hoshin (target a repository's standing epic by name rather than by number; hoshin is the org's hoshin epic in <org>/.github, for /vergil:hoshin's logbook tasks)

docs.title: Intake, planning & deferred
docs.text:
• vrg-intake-create (capture an intake item, linked under its home's intake epic as it is created — no category to choose)
  • vrg-intake-route (apply a review's route: drop, defer, one-off, split, or planning out of intake; defer or drop out of planning; and out of deferred, revive to intake, planning or one-off, refresh, drop, or split. Defer requires --reason and --revisit-when, and is the only way into or out of the deferred queue. size --tasks N --reason TEXT records a planning or deferred item's estimated epic size (an epic-size:<S|M|L|XL> label and a dated Sized … comment), planning --tasks N --reason TEXT sizes an item as it enters planning, and a one-off clears the size. A security item keeps its advisory links when it is transferred, recreated, or split; a split of an item naming several advisories is refused)
  • vrg-queue intake|planning|deferred (the read-only view of one queue — intake oldest first, deferred least recently deferred first — or of all three with a bare vrg-queue; a planning item is held at in-progress, never shown as ready-to-close, while any security advisory still tracks it, or while it is security-labelled and names an advisory that cannot be read, until each advisory is retargeted to the task or tasks that fix it. Planning and deferred lines show each item's epic size (M/14, ? unsized, ! in error), and vrg-queue planning also takes --sort age|size|tasks and --size LIST to order and filter by it. An item whose sizing is in error makes the run exit 2, after the full listing (exit 1 is a queue that could not be read or a usage error). See the vrg-intake-route and vrg-queue reference)
  • vrg-queue adhoc (the read-only view of the ready one-off work: the open tasks under every live ad-hoc epic, grouped by repository and oldest first within each, each with its state — ready, blocked by an open Blocked-by: dependency, or in-flight with the marks that show it, such as an open PR, a report-ready record, a feature branch, a worktree or a merge-review directory. --repo narrows it to one repository's ad-hoc epic. It is not a review queue, so it is shown only when named, never by a bare vrg-queue)
  • vrg-queue hoshin (the same read-only view of the open tasks under the org's hoshin epic; --repo narrows it to one repository's tasks. Like adhoc, it is shown only when named)
  • vrg-security-record (record a security finding as a private draft advisory in <org>/.github, paired with a neutral security-labelled intake issue; create, list, show, retarget (move an advisory's tracking to the tasks that fix it; when they are all in another org, the advisory moves to that org's .github), close (close a draft advisory with a reason posted on every issue it tracks), note (append a dated note to an advisory) and sync (the security-records pass: sync each advisory's state to its issues and report broken pairs, run by the human or the user agent, never on a schedule) — see vergil-tooling's Security Records guide)

An issue still in the intake, planning or deferred queue is not buildable: vrg-pr-workflow report-ready and vrg-submit-pr refuse it until it is routed out.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• vrg-epic-rollup (close a finite epic when its last task closes — event-driven)
  • vrg-finalize-pr (watch the submitted PRs merge, then settle develop once: sync, cleanup, validate and a CD report; it never merges — human, run by every vrg-submit-pr)

docs.title: Reporting & enforcement
docs.text:
• vrg-roadmap (the open-epic roadmap)
  • vrg-epic-audit (drift and invariant violations — read-only, with a gated --close; under --close, run daily by the scheduled sweep, it also runs the orphan pass that attaches every unparented issue to its home's intake epic, except one an outsider opened, which it reports. With --untrusted --since <time> it is instead the read-only outsider report: what accounts outside the trusted roles did in each Vergil org since then, by metadata and links only, with possible tampering first. --close makes no security-advisory call: the security-records pass is vrg-security-record sync, which the read-only vrg-epic-audit only previews)

To relocate a finite epic into its correct home (.github), move the issue with vrg-gh issue transfer and re-link its tasks with vrg-epic-link.

docs.title: Pull-request flow
docs.text:
• vrg-commit (standards-compliant commits)
  • vrg-pr-workflow report-ready (records the PR hand-off)
  • vrg-submit-pr (open the PRs against develop with auto-merge on — squash for one issue, rebase for a batch — then always finalize them; human-run)

docs.title: Merge review
docs.text:
The merge-review skill's tools, run by the agent between a green vrg-validate and report-ready:

  • vrg-merge-review-request (build a review or check request in the task's private directory; it refuses unless the last vrg-validate was a full, clean, green run at HEAD)
  • vrg-merge-review-check (check a stored reviewer result against its request; the skill acts only on a result that passes)

The request builder decides the change class itself, docs-only or code; a docs-only change is reviewed only for merge quality. vrg-change-class is not part of the loop: it prints the class a branch will get, for humans and debugging.

A repository lists its documentation paths for the change class in the [merge-review] docs-paths key of vergil.toml, read as committed at the branch's merge base. The loop, the records and these tools are in vergil-tooling's Merge Review guide.

docs.title: Review decisions
docs.text:
When a review of a task's change needs the human's decision, the decision travels as an authenticated comment on the task issue:

  • vrg-ruling (the agent's side, run as the user identity: request posts a review-decision request, draft relays the reply it drafts for the human, read reads the human's reply with turn checks, and respond posts the response)
  • vrg-ruling-reply (post the human's reply to a request, as the human — human-run in the human's own shell, like vrg-submit-pr)

The merge-review skill sends every stop for the human through them, and epic-implement drafts the human's replies to those stops. The protocol, its checks and recovery are in vergil-tooling's Human Replies guide.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
• vrg-release (cut a release from develop to main — human-run; --resume finishes the open release, and --supersede X.Y.Z replaces an open release that --resume cannot finish)
  • vrg-update-deps (the mechanized dependency update — human-run)
  • vrg-release-record check (read an issue's Released: record and confirm it against git: how a deployment task confirms that a blocked-by task is released)

A release is one workflow, tracked on its release: <version> issue. It runs its stages in order: tag and publish, update-deps, the install stage ([publish].install), a Released: record on every issue the release closes, and last the closing of the tracking issue. A failed stage does not undo what is done: the tracking issue stays open, and the release is always finished with vrg-release --resume, which runs only the stages not yet done. A release that cannot finish is superseded by a new version, which absorbs its issues.

A repository has one release at a time: a fresh vrg-release refuses while any release tracking issue is open. The tracking issue is the human's: it is locked as it is created, and its state is trusted only while every identity that can change it is a human. Any other identity stops the release, which can then only be superseded (the lock and the identity rule).

The update-deps stage runs vrg-update-deps once the release is tagged and published. When anything changed, it opens a deps/update-<next> pull request labelled dependency-update, and a green one is merged. If validation or the merge fails, the PR stays open and a fix task is filed. If an updater itself fails, nothing is pushed and the failure is recorded on the release's tracking issue. Either failure leaves the tracking issue open for --resume. Any open dependency-update PR blocks the next release, until its fix task closes as completed — the next vrg-release then closes the PR and the gate clears. Two flags change this: --allow-pending-deps lets an urgent release through despite an open PR, and the bypass is logged on the release's tracking issue; --without-deps skips the update-deps stage. The release procedure itself is in vergil-tooling's Releasing guide.

The vrg-gh and vrg-git wrappers sit under all of this, enforcing the allow-lists and selecting the right identity; raw git/gh are blocked in agent sessions. The hook guard also refuses an agent's raw issue and PR content reads and names vrg-issue-read, the trusted read command, which prints only what a trusted identity wrote and reports the rest as metadata.

docs.title: The skills, by role
docs.text:
• epic-create — the outer orchestrator of the workflow: brainstorm → epic → spec → spec pushback rounds → human spec review → plan → plan pushback rounds → alignment rounds → docs PR → file tasks, always worked through a planning item that records its progress. Its design-review rounds need paad's unattended runner, paad:paad-delegate, which every box, Lima or cloud, gets by installing paad from the vergil fork through the ordinary plugin refresh. A session without it is on a misconfigured box and runs no review round: epic-create stops and tells the human how to fix the box (paad usage policy §10; paad review rounds: what a session needs).
  • intake-capture — the lossless net: file an intake item with near-zero friction.
  • epic-review — the periodic pass over one queue, in small batches, with a mode per queue:
  • epic-review intake works the intake queue oldest first and routes each item out of it: drop, defer, one-off, split, or planning, or leaves it for now. An item routed to planning is always sized as it moves.
  • epic-review planning keeps the planning queue correct, oldest first: each item is left (most are), deferred, dropped, or, unusually, sent to a repo's ad-hoc epic as a one-off. It prunes and never picks: the human chooses what to plan next and runs epic-create on it. It recommends a size for each waiting item that is unsized or in error, and ends by listing the surviving queue, by size when the human asks.
  • epic-review deferred checks each deferred item's Revisit when: conditions against their real sources and recommends keep, refresh, revive, or drop; an unsized item revived to planning is sized as it moves.
  • epic-implement — the driver above the issue-* skills, run as often as needed between epic-create and epic-retrospective. On the development path it resumes an epic from its issue and plan, dispatches every runnable task to issue-implement, issue-validate or issue-deploy (in parallel sub-agents where that helps, batching small independent code tasks), brings everything that needs the human to one gate, and stops. Its adhoc mode works the ad-hoc tasks instead: org-wide with /vergil:epic-implement adhoc, or for one repository with adhoc --repo <owner>/<repo> or that repository's ad-hoc epic ref. On a development epic it also works the tasks of every proxy epic the epic has in another org. It refuses an epic it does not drive and says what does: given an intake, planning or deferred queue it points to epic-review, which is how a queue is worked; given the hoshin epic, to /vergil:hoshin; and given a proxy epic, to its primary (epic-implement).
  • issue-implement — the agent implements a single issue end-to-end, validates it to green, runs merge-review and hands the PR off with the merge review's eligibility line in its notes, in a Lima or a cloud session alike (issue-implement).
  • merge-review — the pre-PR judgement check issue-implement runs once validation is green: one review by the read-only merge-reviewer agent, at most one fix and check, every stop for the human through vrg-ruling, every raised item closed before hand-off, and an eligibility line for the PR notes (merge-review).
  • fixture-run — files a fixture run on one or more of the language fixture repos: per fixture, a change, release and validation trio, blocked by the release or deployment task passed as --after. It files the tasks and never runs them. An epic whose plan changes language support, container images, shared CI workflows or release tooling seeds one run per affected fixture (fixture-run).
  • hoshin — runs the hoshin kanri review cadence with the human and writes its public logbook: /vergil:hoshin start each working day works out which reviews are due, closes any period left open (late, or recorded as not performed) and runs the daily review and any boundary reviews; end or end <level> is optional. The daily review also shows two trust checks, in the terminal only: the outsider report (vrg-epic-audit --untrusted) and the result of the nightly trusted-authors check. Each run files the follow-ups the human decides on and hands off one docs PR of dated entries, after a security screen and the human's approval of the full text. Its Logbook: task lives under the org's hoshin epic, and it skips merge-review on purpose, so its handoff carries no eligibility line (hoshin).
  • pr-watch — the agent monitors an open PR through CI and review, reconciling until it is mergeable. It fixes a logbook PR (one titled Logbook:) like any other, but skips the merge review of its fixes, as the logbook run itself does: the text passed the run's security screen and the human's approval before the PR existed, and a fix to it is mechanical, never new content.

Together, the tools give the mechanical guarantees and the skills give the process on top of them — which is exactly why the story belongs here, in one place, while each tool's and action's mechanical detail stays in its own repo.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: Getting an idea into shipped, closed tasks is a pipeline — and the whole bet is that front-loading the analysis makes the implementation near-bulletproof. Hours spent up front on design and planning pay for themselves when the pull requests just work the first time.

docs.title: epic-create is the entry point
docs.text:
For non-trivial work, the starting move is epic-create, not brainstorming directly. A solution worth thinking through is worth recording as work, so there is little value in designing something and then walking away from it untracked. epic-create opens into brainstorming and orchestrates the whole sequence. If the design collapses to a trivial, single-PR change, it is a task, not an epic — filed under the target repository's ad-hoc epic, and done.

Every run is tracked in a planning item — an issue in the planning queue that records its own epic creation, with progress comments so a session can pause and resume days later:

  • epic-create <issue> starts or resumes that planning item (an intake or deferred item is first moved to the planning queue).
  • epic-create with a free-text idea first turns the idea into a new planning item.
  • epic-create with no argument summarizes the planning queue and asks which item to work on.

Choosing which item to plan next is the human's act: they pick it and run epic-create on it, picking only what will be implemented soon, since a plan left sitting goes stale. epic-review planning does not choose; it keeps the planning queue correct. Each item that is still valid stays, and the rest are deferred, dropped or, unusually, sent to a repo's ad-hoc epic as a one-off. The pass ends by listing the surviving queue to help the human choose. A planning item can carry an estimated epic size (S, M, L or XL). Sizing is optional: an unsized item shows ? in vrg-queue. For the small-end cadence, vrg-queue planning --sort size --size S lists the small items (an estimated 1–9 tasks), oldest first, and any item whose sizing is in error (!), which is always listed whatever the filter.

The planning item closes once the epic exists, its docs task has merged, and its tasks are filed — "planned as" the epic it became.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
epic-create drives these stages in order:

  1. Brainstorm — explore intent and converge on an approved design.
  2. Initialize — create the epic in .github and seed its bookend tasks (documentation first; documentation review and the retrospective last).
  3. Spec → spec pushback rounds → human review — write the spec, critique it adversarially in spec pushback rounds, and have a human review it.
  4. Plan → plan pushback rounds → alignment rounds — write the implementation plan in one automated pass, critique it in plan pushback rounds, then reconcile the spec and the plan in alignment rounds, which may change both.
  5. Docs PR — land the spec and plan as a single documentation PR (which closes the documentation bookend).
  6. File tasks — create the implementation tasks from the plan, each in the repository where its PR will land.

The review steps in stages 3 and 4 run in human-gated rounds, described below.

docs.title: The interaction doctrine
docs.text:
The design and review steps are not hand-waving — each runs a concrete, reusable skill, composed from two packages: Superpowers (brainstorming, writing-plans) and PAAD (pushback, alignment). Brainstorming produces the spec, pushback critiques the spec, writing-plans generates the plan, pushback critiques the plan, and alignment confirms the spec and the plan match. The pipeline mixes interactive, human-gated and automated stages on purpose:

Stage Mode Contract superpowers:brainstorming interactive Explore intent, one question at a time — produces the spec. Design review (pushback on the spec, pushback on the plan, alignment) human-gated rounds A fresh review-only subagent per round, run by paad's unattended runner. The main session walks the human through the findings, and the human decides every further round. superpowers:writing-plans automated Generate the implementation plan in one pass; no gating.

Each design-review round reviews the whole document, and the main session records it as a comment on the planning item. The human decides every finding and whether to run another round of the stage. The rules are in the paad review doctrine, mode 1. How the workflow uses PAAD, and every place it deviates from the PAAD authors' recommendations, is recorded in the paad usage policy.

Every design-review round needs paad's unattended runner, paad:paad-delegate. Every box, the host, Lima VMs and cloud VMs alike, installs paad from the vergil fork through the ordinary plugin refresh, so every session has the delegate. A session without it is on a misconfigured box and runs no review round: epic-create stops and tells the human how to fix the box (paad usage policy §10; doctrine §1.8; paad review rounds: what a session needs).

The human-judgment principle governs brainstorming: stop and ask only for ambiguities or judgment calls that materially affect the outcome; handle minor, obvious corrections by batching them to the end as a single "here are the no-brainers — correct me if I'm wrong" review, rather than gating each one.

Design review walks the findings one at a time, in severity order, except for one batch at the end: low findings, each with its own decision, and known findings, which keep their earlier decision unless the human pulls one out (doctrine §2.2, step 4).

The goal of all this front-loading is blunt: plans that just work — on the order of 90–99% of tasks green on first implementation. Real-world misses still happen and get patched, but the more upfront refinement, the higher the success rate, and the more mechanical work can eventually be forked off and trusted to run on its own.

Each task is then implemented with the issue-implement skill, which implements the issue, validates it to green and hands the PR off to the human. Between a green vrg-validate and the hand-off with report-ready, it runs the merge-review skill: one review of the change by the read-only merge-reviewer agent, at most one fix and a check of that fix, and every stop for the human through an authenticated vrg-ruling request on the task issue. Its eligibility line goes into the PR notes. The detail is in vergil-tooling's Merge Review guide.

Given a list of small issues of one epic in one repository, issue-implement implements them as one batch: one branch, one commit per issue, each issue validated and merge-reviewed on its own, and one hand-off that becomes one PR with a Closes line per issue. epic-implement may batch independent small ready tasks the same way. What may be batched, and how a batch is stopped or resumed, is in the plugin's issue-implement reference and the skill's Batch mode section.

Merge review is not paad: issue-implement runs no paad review of its own, so it works the same in a Lima or a cloud session; paad's review rounds belong to design review in epic-create.

docs.title: Working the ad-hoc tasks
docs.text:
Not every ready task belongs to a planned epic: a one-off routed out of a queue, or a design that collapsed to a single PR, is a task under its repository's ad-hoc epic. Those tasks are worked with epic-implement in its adhoc mode — org-wide with /vergil:epic-implement adhoc, or for one repository with adhoc --repo <owner>/<repo> or that repository's ad-hoc epic ref.

Ad-hoc tasks are standalone work only, each picked up, merged and released on its own. Two kinds of ready task that are not standalone have homes of their own, and epic-implement refuses both epics:

  • Hoshin's logbook tasks sit under the org's hoshin epic. Given it, epic-implement stops and points to /vergil:hoshin, which files and works them.

  • Another org's epic tasks sit under that epic's proxy. Given a proxy, epic-implement stops and points to its primary: running it on the primary works the proxy's tasks beside the primary's own.

  • Collect. It gathers the open tasks under the ad-hoc epics with vrg-queue adhoc and summarizes them by repository. A task already handed off or worked elsewhere (an open PR, a report-ready record, a remote branch) is left alone; one that stopped on this machine is resumed the way the development path resumes a task.

  • Propose a strategy. There is no plan to set an order, so it proposes one: which tasks to batch together per repository, which to run alone, which to leave for later, and the order, oldest first unless there is a reason to differ. Ad-hoc tasks are filed one at a time and rarely say what they depend on, so the strategy judges overlap explicitly — tasks that touch the same files are batched or run one after another — and names which tasks run at the same time.
  • One confirmation. The human confirms the whole strategy once.
  • Dispatch and gate. It dispatches the tasks under the same gates, ruling relay and batching rules as a development epic, brings everything that needs the human to one gate, and stops. Its records go on the ad-hoc epic of the repository concerned.

The adhoc mode reads no plan and drafts no retrospective: an ad-hoc epic has no plan and never closes. Like the development path, it is stateless, so re-running it re-derives where things stand from GitHub.
